papers.title: Projeto e fabricação de um motor didático como proposta de PBL
papers.abstract: A Aprendizagem Baseada em Projetos – do inglês Project Based Learning - (PBL) é uma metodologia de ensino ativa que visa o aprendizado dos alunos envolvendo-os em projetos que desenvolvam os temas tratados nas disciplinas. A literatura apresenta casos de sucessos da aplicação do PBL nas áreas de engenharia, medicina, física dentre outras. Na Engenharia Mecânica e de Produção, há diversas máquinas, equipamentos e sistemas que podem ser desenvolvidos a fim de consolidar os conhecimentos adquiridos no curso. Nesse contexto, o motor à combustão interna é uma máquina muito difundida e pode permitir a fixação de vários conhecimentos abordados nesses cursos. Nesse cenário, o objetivo desta pesquisa é o de projetar e fabricar um modelo didático de motor monocilíndrico à combustão e aplicá-lo como um PBL para o desenvolvimento das competências dos alunos ao longo do curso. O termo modelo didático, nesta aplicação, refere-se a um modelo que possa reproduzir os mecanismos de movimento das principais partes do motor, sem a aplicação da transferência de energia química/térmica em energia mecânica (movimento). Logo, seu funcionamento se dá de forma manual. O projeto do motor foi concebido considerando seus principais componentes. Esses foram modelados no software CAD Inventor e fabricados em máquinas como torno, fresadora, impressora 3D entre outras máquinas disponíveis na instituição. Como resultado da presente pesquisa, tem-se um protótipo de um modelo didático de motor à combustão monocilíndrico que pode ser utilizado para materializar os conhecimentos adquiridos no curso de Engenharia Mecânica e Produção. Palavras-chave: PBL; metodologia ativa; modelo didático; motor. Abstract Project-Based Learning (PBL) is an active teaching methodology that engages students in projects designed to develop the topics covered in academic disciplines. The literature reports successful applications of PBL in engineering, medicine, physics, and several other fields. In Mechanical and Production Engineering, students can develop a wide range of machines, equipment, and systems to consolidate the knowledge acquired throughout the course. Among these, the internal combustion engine stands out as a widely used machine that helps reinforce several engineering concepts. This research aims to design and manufacture a didactic model of a single-cylinder internal combustion engine and use it as a PBL activity to foster the development of students’ competencies throughout the program. In this study, the term “didactic model” refers to a model that reproduces the motion mechanisms of the engine’s main components without converting chemical and thermal energy into mechanical energy. Therefore, the model operates manually. The project team designed the engine based on its main components. They modeled the parts using Autodesk Inventor CAD software and manufactured them with lathes, milling machines, 3D printers, and other equipment available at the institution. The project resulted in a functional prototype of a single-cylinder internal combustion engine didactic model that supports the visualization and practical application of concepts taught in Mechanical and Production Engineering courses. Keywords: Project-Based Learning (PBL); active learning; didactic model; internal combustion engine. Resume El Aprendizaje Basado en Proyectos (ABP) es una metodología de enseñanza activa que busca involucrar a los estudiantes en proyectos que desarrollan los temas tratados en las disciplinas. La literatura presenta casos exitosos de aplicación del ABP en áreas como ingeniería, medicina, física, entre otras. En Ingeniería Mecánica y de Producción, existen diversas máquinas, equipos y sistemas que pueden desarrollarse para consolidar los conocimientos adquiridos en el curso. En este contexto, el motor de combustión interna es una máquina ampliamente utilizada que puede permitir la consolidación de diversos conocimientos abordados en estos cursos. En este contexto, el objetivo de esta investigación es diseñar y fabricar un modelo didáctico de un motor de combustión interna monocilíndrico y aplicarlo como ABP para el desarrollo de las competencias de los estudiantes a lo largo del curso. El término "modelo didáctico", en esta aplicación, se refiere a un modelo que puede reproducir los mecanismos de movimiento de las partes principales del motor sin aplicar la conversión de energía química/térmica en energía mecánica (movimiento). Por lo tanto, su operación es manual. El diseño del motor se concibió considerando sus componentes principales. Estos se modelaron en el software CAD Inventor y se fabricaron utilizando máquinas como tornos, fresadoras, impresoras 3D y otras disponibles en la institución. Como resultado de esta investigación, se desarrolló un prototipo de modelo didáctico de un motor de combustión interna monocilíndrico, que permite materializar los conocimientos adquiridos en el curso de Ingeniería Mecánica y de Producción. Palabras clave: ABP; metodología activa; modelo didáctico; motor.

papers.title: Biomechanical evaluation of screw-supported prostheses in reconstructing Paprosky IIIB acetabular defects
papers.abstract: Paprosky IIIB acetabular defects represent one of the most severe forms of bone loss, often reconstructed using custom-made triflange acetabular components (CTAC). However, traditional CTACs might exhibit insufficient stability under extensive bone loss. Building on the use of long column screws in acetabular reconstruction, this study proposed and biomechanically evaluated a screw-supported acetabular prosthesis based on pile-foundation principles for the reconstruction of Paprosky IIIB acetabular defects. Based on defect morphology, three implants were modeled: a standard triflange cup, an enhanced triflange cup and a screw-supported prosthesis. Finite element analysis (FEA) was conducted under three physiological loading conditions: walking, stair ascent, and stair descent. Von Mises stress, bone strain, and interface micromotion were used to assess mechanical performance. Mechanical compression tests validated the FEA results. The results indicated that the screw-supported prosthesis showed lower, more evenly distributed stresses, a broader strain area within the bone regeneration range, and smaller micromotion in posterior column defects. In anterior column defects, it demonstrated lower peak stresses and improved micromotion. Biomechanical experimental results aligned with the FEA outcomes. This design provided a biomechanically solution for individualized acetabular reconstruction, particularly for posterior column defects, and validated the application of pile foundation principles in orthopedic implant design.

papers.title: Material–interface trade-offs in biomaterial-based femoral head reconstruction for osteonecrosis: A finite element comparison
papers.abstract: Early stability after femoral head reconstruction reflects implant stiffness, interface fixation, and load-transfer geometry, yet these effects are difficult to separate clinically. We compared four reconstructions in one computed tomography–derived femur with heterogeneous bone properties and a standardised weight-bearing lesion (∼35% of femoral-head volume). Heel strike (HS), mid-stance (MS), and toe-off (TO) were simulated for an isolated fibular strut, screw-augmented strut, porous tantalum rod, and porous β-tricalcium phosphate rod. The screw-augmented strut produced the lowest displacement (1.393–2.108 mm) and subchondral stress (92.3–125.3 MPa), whereas the isolated strut had the lowest mean micromotion (0.080 mm). The β-tricalcium phosphate rod had the lowest implant tensile stress (1.109–1.994 MPa) but the greatest displacement and micromotion. In the tantalum model, increasing interface friction from 0.2 to 0.5 reduced micromotion by 9.4–13.7%, while displacement and subchondral stress changed by < 0.2%. Scenario weighting favoured the screw-augmented strut for collapse resistance and the isolated strut for interface stability. Within this standardised model, performance reflected trade-offs among support, fixation, and material stress rather than stiffness alone. Experimental validation and patient-specific modelling remain necessary before clinical translation.

papers.title: Mapping Analysis to Predict the Associated EQ-5D-3L Utility Values from the Oxford Hip Score
papers.abstract: Purpose: The aim was to assess mapping models to predict the EQ-5D-3L utility from the Oxford hip score (OHS) and validate these before and after total hip arthroplasty (THA). Methods: Separate retrospective cohorts of patients who had undergone THA in different centres were used to create (n = 3981) and validate (n = 7168) the prediction models. Patient demographics, body mass index (BMI), OHS and EQ-5D were collected preoperatively and one year postoperatively. Predictive models were formulated using generalised linear regression. Results: In the modelling cohort, mean OHS improved from 20.8 preoperatively to 39.6 postoperatively; the mean EQ-5D improved from 0.391 preoperatively to 0.788 postoperatively. Significant (p < 0.001) correlations were observed between OHS and EQ-5D preoperatively (r = 0.690) and postoperatively (r = 0.777) and for change (r = 0.611) and combined scores (r = 0.812). Four models predicting EQ-5D from OHS explained 38.5% to 65.9% of the variance. Age and BMI did not improve model fit. Predicted mean EQ-5D utilities differed statistically from observed values for most models, but all differences were below the minimal clinical important difference (MCID). Including individual OHS items marginally improved performance (<2%). External validation showed good agreement at the cohort level but lower accuracy for individual-level prediction (27.7% for change to 65.0% for postoperative scores to be within the MCID). Conclusions: The EQ-5D-3L utility index, on a cohort level, may be reliably estimated from the OHS. Predicted individual patient utility error beyond the MCID varied from one-third to more than two-thirds depending on the data assessed and so should not be employed for this purpose on a patient level.

papers.title: Beyond Porosity: Topology-Dependent Mechanical Response of PLA TPMS Structures Under Bone Scaffold Design Constraints
papers.abstract: The design of triply periodic minimal surface (TPMS) structures for bone scaffolds often relies on comparisons at fixed porosity. In extrusion-based fabrication, however, changing cell size while holding the wall thickness constant couples porosity, pore size, and cell scale. This study compared sheet-based Gyroid, Diamond, and Primitive architectures fabricated from commercial PLA + HS using fused deposition modeling. The design included 22 configurations, five specimens per configuration, a nominal wall thickness of 0.20 mm, and design porosities of 44.4–78.5%. Gravimetric measurements revealed topology-dependent deviations from the designed solid fraction but could not establish internal geometric fidelity. The apparent elastic modulus ranged from 74.30 to 605.06 MPa and first-peak compressive strength from 1.59 to 16.82 MPa. Analysis of covariance revealed significant topology-by-porosity interactions. Diamond generally exhibited the highest stiffness and strength, with its separation from Gyroid narrowing toward higher porosity. Gibson–Ashby fits captured topology-dependent stiffness scaling within the tested domain. These findings support mechanical architecture selection under common manufacturing and loading conditions, without establishing biological efficacy or the suitability of the commercial filament for implantation.

papers.title: Data-driven discovery of water-splitting electrocatalysts: From predictive machine learning to autonomous optimization
papers.abstract: Machine learning is reshaping the design of water-splitting electrocatalysts by enabling data-driven exploration of structure-property relationships beyond conventional trial-and-error approaches. By integrating physically meaningful descriptors with predictive algorithms, ML provides a pathway to accelerate catalyst optimization and uncover underlying reaction mechanisms. Descriptor engineering plays a central role, combining morphological and structural features, composition-dependent chemical descriptors, and electronic structure parameters such as d-band center, density of states, work function, and adsorption energies, together with synthesis-dependent variables linking preparation conditions to performance. On this basis, diverse learning strategies including supervised regression models, ensemble methods, unsupervised clustering, Bayesian optimization, active learning, and deep learning architectures have been employed to navigate complex materials spaces efficiently. Emerging physics-informed and symbolic learning approaches further enhance interpretability while maintaining predictive power. Collectively, these advances accelerate rational catalyst discovery for hydrogen and oxygen evolution reactions, improving efficiency in sustainable hydrogen production.

papers.title: Machine Learning Prediction and Interpretability Analysis of the Unconfined Compressive Strength of Alkali-Activated Stabilized Soft Soil Under Coupled Wetting–Drying Cycles and Acid Attack
papers.abstract: Predicting the unconfined compressive strength (UCS) of alkali-activated stabilized soft soil under coupled acid attack and wetting–drying cycles requires evaluation across correlated laboratory observations. This study analyzed 689 records from 53 complete mixtures, with seven material and environmental inputs, using four machine-learning models (DT, RF, SVM, and XGBoost) and four neural models (PINN, BPNN, CNN, and LSTM). Generalization to previously unseen mixtures was evaluated by five-fold outer GroupKFold with three-fold mixture-grouped tuning. Each original record contributed one out-of-fold prediction. The pooled grouped-CV R2 values ranged from 0.5043 to 0.7605, with RMSEs of 0.3579–0.5148 MPa. XGBoost attained the highest point estimate (R2=0.7605; RMSE = 0.3579 MPa), followed by SVM (R2=0.7362; RMSE = 0.3756 MPa). PINN and its architecture-matched BPNN produced identical grouped-CV predictions and no demonstrated incremental benefit. A prospective penalty-activation diagnostic confirmed that soft penalties can affect training trajectories but did not reconstruct the archived model-selection runs. A separately tuned, five-step, structure-matched ablation found no additional predictive gain from preceding design covariates in CNN and LSTM. Historical fixed-configuration random-CV comparisons were removed because the original hyperparameter-selection provenance could not be verified. SHAP and partial dependence analyses describe model-learned associations, and SEM offers qualitative morphological context. These models provide preliminary screening aids within the tested materials and factor levels, not engineering design tools; independent batch and field validation remains necessary.

papers.title: Edge Intelligence for Field-Deployable Plant Disease Detection: A Critical Review of Lightweight Models, Adaptation, and Uncertainty-Aware Learning, with Implications for Pomegranate
papers.abstract: Introduction: While laboratory-trained models are highly accurate, several factors can affect the accuracy of models in the field, such as changes in lighting, background noise, plant growth stage, and imaging conditions. In this review, emphasis will be placed on robust and efficient edge-intelligence approaches for detecting pomegranate diseases. Methods: Based on PRISMA, eight aspects were covered: lightweight CNN/YOLO models, Kolmogorov-Arnold networks, Mamba-based models, domain and test-time adaptation, uncertainty quantification, foundation models, model compression, and multimodal sensor fusion. Of these studies, 108 were published within the last six years (2020-2026), and three were fundamental studies. Results: Emphasis is placed on the trade-offs between accuracy, computational efficiency, adaptation stability, and uncertainty calibration. While lightweight models fail to capture the small lesions, heavy models are computationally expensive; state-space models and test-time adaptation either lose local information or suffer from compounding errors under distribution shift. Running and managing foundation models on resource-limited edge devices is also challenging. Discussion: While most studies have investigated one challenge, there are a couple of studies that have combined visual features with bioimpedance and/or temporal (weather) data to detect presymptomatic features. This shows the need for integrated architectures that involve efficient representation learning, model compression, model adaptation, multimodal sensing, and riskaware prediction. Conclusion: PomStage-Net, a conceptual framework (not yet experimentally validated), is proposed for lightweight, temporally ordinal, and uncertainty-calibrated detection of pomegranate diseases. Future research should focus on causally inspired multimodal sensor fusion, adaptive learning, and uncertainty characterization to achieve reliable, real-time, fielddeployable agricultural diagnosis.

papers.title: A Review of Indoor Navigation Methods for Autonomous Mobile Robots: From Path Planning to Large Model-Based Decision-Making
papers.abstract: Indoor navigation is fundamental to autonomous mobile robots (AMRs), yet the relationships between explicit planning, learned policies, and large model-based decision-making remain difficult to assess across heterogeneous experiments. This review establishes a unified taxonomy of path planning-based, learning-based, and large model-based navigation according to their dominant decision-making mechanisms, while recognizing hybrid systems. We summarize the foundations of simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM), deep and reinforcement learning, and large models, then examine representative methods through their navigation tasks, decision roles, and validation settings. To move beyond qualitative comparisons, we synthesize reported quantitative evidence on navigation success, computational cost, online latency, dynamic adaptability, physical validation, and safety, explicitly distinguishing task protocols and measurement boundaries. We also compare common simulation platforms, datasets, and physical-robot platforms, examining how sensor noise, moving obstacles, and execution uncertainty affect sim-to-real transfer. The analysis shows that explicit planning provides interpretable, constraint-aware motion generation, learned policies support experience-driven adaptation, and large models enable semantic instruction understanding and high-level task reasoning. However, no paradigm alone resolves the challenges of generalization, embodied grounding, inference delay, and reliable physical deployment. Rather than ranking methods across incomparable evaluations, we identify complementary capabilities and the value of hybrid architectures that couple semantic reasoning with constraint-checked low-level execution and feedback. Future work should address lifelong adaptation, embodied memory and world models, efficient inference, and measurable safety and failure recovery.

papers.title: Efficient Thermal Analysis of On-Orbit Satellites Using a Nondimensionalized Physics-Informed Neural Network
papers.abstract: This study proposes a nondimensional physics-informed neural network (Nd-PINN) framework for predicting the infrared radiation characteristics of low-Earth-orbit satellites under complex space thermal environments. The Laplace heat conduction equation and nonlinear boundary conditions involving solar irradiation, Earth albedo, and Earth infrared radiation are embedded into the loss function, while nondimensional preprocessing improves training stability by balancing residual magnitudes. Four numerical cases of increasing complexity were used for validation. For cases with analytical solutions, Nd-PINN achieved absolute temperature errors below 0.2 K, relative infrared radiation errors below 0.3%, and energy conservation errors below 0.001%. Under unidirectional solar irradiation, the model shows good consistency with the azimuthal temperature gradient predicted by Lambert’s cosine law, with an energy conservation error below 0.58%. In the multi-source coupled radiation case, it maintained strong physical consistency, with an energy conservation error below 0.54%. These results demonstrate that Nd-PINN can effectively solve both linear and strongly nonlinear thermal problems without complex meshing, while providing continuous and smooth global temperature fields. The proposed framework offers an accurate, mesh-free alternative for satellite thermal analysis and infrared feature identification.

papers.title: Managing periprosthetic joint infection through the direct anterior approach: Partial two-stage exchange with femoral stem retention
papers.abstract: Periprosthetic joint infection (PJI) remains a devastating complication of total hip arthroplasty (THA), and chronic PJI in the presence of a well-fixed femoral stem is particularly challenging because removal of an osseointegrated stem carries substantial morbidity. Partial two-stage exchange (P2-SE) with femoral stem retention, in which the acetabular components are removed and replaced with an antibiotic-cement functional spacer while the well-fixed stem is retained and debrided, has emerged as an alternative to complete one-stage or two-stage exchange. The direct anterior approach (DAA), although widely adopted for primary THA, has rarely been described for the management of PJI. This article reports three cases of chronic PJI managed by P2-SE performed entirely through the original anterior interval, together with a comprehensive review of the published outcomes of P2-SE. Two of the three patients achieved infection control and were pain-free and ambulatory at final follow-up with an antibiotic-loaded cemented acetabular construct (a polyethylene liner with a modular ceramic head in one, a dual-mobility construct in the other), and did not require second-stage reimplantation, while the third patient developed a recurrent infection after cessation of oral suppression and was subsequently converted to a formal two-stage exchange. The accompanying literature review demonstrates infection eradication rates of approximately 81 to 100% across predominantly Level IV series, with reported outcomes comparable to those of complete two-stage exchange. P2-SE through the DAA appears to be a reasonable option in carefully selected patients with a well-fixed femoral stem, although further prospective comparative investigation is warranted.

papers.title: A Deep Reinforcement learning approach for Profit-Maximizing and robust control of hybrid CSP-PV plants with Power-to-Heat integration
papers.abstract: The optimal operation of hybrid Concentrated Solar Power (CSP) and Photovoltaic (PV) plants is a challenging task due to the stochastic nature of solar irradiance, volatile electricity prices, and the complex coupling between Thermal Energy Storage (TES), Power Block (PB), and power-to-heat devices. This study proposes a model-free Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) agent, trained using Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), to dynamically dispatch energy flows in a CSP-PV plant equipped with a parallel electric heater and two-tank TES. The agent is trained from scratch in a high-fidelity simulation environment, without access to future information, using historical weather and market data from Spain. The learned policy achieves stable convergence with a coefficient of variation of 0.0768 in returns across independent runs. Extensive testing on unseen real and synthetic scenarios confirms generalization and robustness to distributional shifts in prices and weather. On average across all evaluated scenarios, the DRL controller increases net operational profit by 10% and reduces PB startups by 13% compared to a conventional heuristic based on current operating conditions. Remarkably, its net profit is only 2.5% lower than that of a perfect-foresight heuristic with advance knowledge of the actual daily electricity prices, but with 29% fewer PB startups, demonstrating a superior trade-off between economic performance and system durability. These results highlight the potential of DRL as a viable, generalizable, and cost-effective control solution for next-generation hybrid solar plants, contributing to enhanced grid integration and reduced operational risks.

papers.title: Advances in cartilage tissue engineering: Strategies, challenges, and future directions.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND AND AIM: Articular cartilage is highly susceptible to physical and degenerative damage due to its avascular nature and limited regenerative capacity. The aim of this review article is to explore recent advances in cartilage tissue engineering to develop alternative therapeutic approaches for repairing damaged tissues. STUDY METHOD: A structured search was conducted across scientific databases-including PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science-to identify relevant studies published between 2000 and 2026 regarding cartilage tissue engineering. The search covered topics such as cell sources, biomaterial scaffolds, growth factors, bioreactor systems, and emerging cartilage regeneration strategies, utilizing a combination of keywords and terms related to cartilage tissue engineering, cartilage regeneration, biomaterials, scaffolds, hydrogels, stem cells, chondrogenesis, and 3D bioprinting. Retrieved studies were screened for relevance to the review's scope, and eligible studies were qualitatively analyzed and synthesized to summarize recent advancements, existing challenges, and future directions in the field of cartilage tissue engineering. As this study was designed as a narrative review, no formal meta-analysis or quantitative statistical synthesis was performed. FINDINGS: The findings indicate that the use of mesenchymal stem cells, nanostructured scaffolds with bioactive compositions, and the application of mechanical and chemical factors play a significant role in cell differentiation into chondrocytes and successful cartilage regeneration. However, challenges such as mechanical integrity, long-term durability, and clinical translation still remain. CONCLUSION: Cartilage tissue engineering holds great potential for the treatment of cartilage injuries; nevertheless, further studies are needed to optimize cell sources, scaffold design, and environmental control conditions in the tissue engineering process to achieve effective clinical applications.

papers.title: Generalized and scalable deep Gaussian process emulation
papers.abstract: Gaussian process (GP) emulators have become essential tools for approximating complex simulators, significantly reducing computational demands in optimization, sensitivity analysis, and model calibration. While traditional GP emulators effectively model continuous and Gaussian-distributed simulator outputs with homogeneous variability, they typically struggle with discrete, heteroskedastic Gaussian, or non-Gaussian data, limiting their applicability to increasingly common stochastic simulators. A scalable Generalized Deep Gaussian Process (GDGP) emulation framework is introduced to accommodate simulators with heteroskedastic Gaussian outputs and a wide range of non-Gaussian response distributions, including Poisson, negative binomial, and categorical distributions. The GDGP framework leverages the expressiveness of DGPs and extends them to latent GP structures, enabling it to capture the complex, non-stationary behavior inherent in many simulators while also modeling non-Gaussian simulator outputs. GDGP is made scalable by incorporating the Vecchia approximation for settings with a large number of input locations, while also developing efficient inference procedures for handling large numbers of replicates. In particular, methodological developments are presented that further enhance the computation of the approach for heteroskedastic Gaussian responses. A series of synthetic and empirical examples demonstrates that these extensions deliver the practical application of GDGP emulators and a unified methodology capable of addressing diverse modeling challenges. The proposed GDGP framework is implemented in the open-source R package dgpsi .

papers.title: Beyond Accuracy: A Cost-Aware Perspective on Hyperparameter Optimization — A Survey and Gap Analysis
papers.abstract: Hyperparameter optimization (HPO) methods are usually compared by the best score they reach after a fixed number of trials.That number says nothing about how quickly a method improves as time, money or energy is spent.This paper surveys HPO methods with cost in mind, points out that the scoreversus-cost record of a search is rarely reported, and suggests reporting it as a Performance-per-Cost Curve (PpCC) with a few summary numbers.To see whether this matters, four methods (grid search, random search, Gaussian-process Bayesian optimization and the tree-structured Parzen estimator) were run on three classification tasks, ten times each.The two Bayesian methods got the highest cross-validation scores, and the tree-structured Parzen estimator beat grid and random search by a clear margin on two of the three datasets.On held-out test data, though, the differences were small and mostly within chance.On one dataset the ranking of the methods changed depending on the budget.Equal numbers of trials also did not mean equal cost: total search time differed by up to about 13% between methods.The extra computation of the Bayesian methods was under 1% of total cost here.The results argue for reporting the whole score-versus-cost record of a search and not just its final score.

papers.title: Digital twin-driven congestion-aware route planning for intelligent transportation systems
papers.abstract: With the rapid advancement of autonomous driving and navigation technologies, an increasing number of vehicles rely on real-time routing services such as Google Maps and Waze. However, these services frequently fail to improve aggregate traffic conditions, as rerouting drivers based on existing congestion amplifies herding behavior and produces new secondary bottlenecks. To address this issue, a digital twin-based dynamic route-planning framework is proposed, in which real-time vehicle detection, surrogate-modeled traffic-flow prediction, and a congestion-aware metaheuristic router are integrated into a closed-loop pipeline. A network of intersection cameras with a YOLOv8 detector supplies real-time inflow and outflow data, which is fed into a Lighthill–Whitham–Richards (LWR)-based simulator incorporating signal, lane, and weather factors. The counting stage is validated at the level of individual crossing events on continuously annotated traffic sequences. To deliver real-time predictions at network scale, a parallel partial Gaussian stochastic process (PP-GaSP) surrogate is adapted to edge-level traffic volumes, providing sub-millisecond predictions with closed-form Student- t uncertainty that the router consumes as a risk-inflated flow estimate. Since the single-vehicle social-cost objective is edge-separable and solved exactly by a modified Dijkstra search, the paper addresses routing where herding actually arises, jointly optimizing a batch of concurrent demand streams whose coupled objective contains a non-separable network-bottleneck term beyond the reach of per-vehicle best-response methods. A new metaheuristic, Adaptive Chaotic Bacterial Foraging Optimization (ACBFO) is proposed to solve the batch problem through congestion-guided chemotaxis, which reroutes demand streams off the current fleet bottleneck within a chaotically scheduled bacterial foraging search. In paired experiments, ACBFO attains the provably optimal single-vehicle solution on every instance and significantly outperforms exact sequential routing, iterated best response, and metaheuristic and learning-based baselines, with the largest gains on the fleet bottleneck ratio, and a multi-window closed-loop replay exercises the prediction, joint-routing, and feedback stages under time-varying boundary-count inputs.

papers.title: AI-Powered Robotics for Reliable, Stable, and Robust Operation and Maintenance of Power Systems: Architecture, Unified Modeling, and Quantitative Evaluation
papers.abstract: Robotic inspection and artificial intelligence (AI) are increasingly used in power-system operation and maintenance (O&M), yet they are usually evaluated in isolation—by image-detection accuracy or robot mobility—rather than by their effect on the quantities utilities are regulated on. This paper proposes AIRO-PS, a standards-aligned six-layer architecture that integrates aerial, line-mounted, substation, and live-line robots with edge AI, zoned communications, and a network digital twin, together with a unified modeling framework that maps each robotic or AI capability to reliability, stability, and robustness parameters: pre-failure detection probability, effective failure rate, restoration-time components, dynamic thermal rating, critical-clearing-time margin, and guaranteed control error. The framework is evaluated through eight coupled simulation studies and a techno-economic appraisal. On an 11-kV test feeder, a 6000-year sequential Monte Carlo simulation shows that AI-robotic O&M reduces SAIFI by 67.3%, SAIDI by 83.8%, and expected energy not supplied by 84.1% relative to conventional O&M, and lowers the 90th-percentile annual SAIDI by 77.1%. Robot-sensed dynamic line rating raises mean ampacity by 36.8% under hot-climate conditions, a multilayer-perceptron transient-stability classifier reaches 98.85% accuracy, Bayesian prognostics with monthly robotic data cut remaining-useful-life error by 86%, a Q-learning maintenance policy performs within 1.5% of the average-cost optimum, and sliding-mode stand-off control reduces unmanned-aerial-vehicle tracking error near live conductors by 89%. A 250-feeder deployment yields an internal rate of return of 31.1%.

papers.title: Unveiling adsorption sites and proton transfer pathways for glycerol at low-coordinated CaO sites through active-learning-guided DFTB sampling and DFT refinement
papers.abstract: In this study, we combine active learning (AL), density functional tight-binding (DFTB), and dispersion-corrected density functional theory (DFT-D3) to investigate glycerol adsorption at reactive CaO sites modeled by a (CaO) 16 cluster. The AL-DFTB stage identifies low-energy adsorption candidates, which are then refined at the DFT-D3 level. The optimized structures consistently show chemisorption via coordination of two glycerol oxygen atoms to Ca 2+ centers, accompanied by spontaneous transfer of a hydroxyl proton to a basic O 2- site. The most stable complex has an adsorption free energy of approximately -32.0 kcal/mol. A periodic PBE-D3 calculation on CaO(001) reproduces the same qualitative binding motif and spontaneous deprotonation, supporting the robustness of the mechanistic picture and showing that adsorption energies depend on the coordination environment of the surface sites. Climbing-image nudged elastic band calculations further indicate that a second proton transfer proceeds with a very low barrier. Complementary ELF and VDD analyses show that this step is facilitated by a short hydrogen bond and the oxide site's strong basicity. Overall, the results identify low-coordinated CaO motifs as efficient basic sites for sequential glycerol deprotonation and demonstrate that the AL-DFTB/DFT-D3 workflow is a practical strategy for exploring adsorption and activation processes at oxide catalytic sites.

summary_zh.validation: 以周期性PBE-D3计算和ELF/VDD电子结构分析交叉验证。

summary_en.motivation: The study aims to clarify how glycerol adsorbs and deprotonates at reactive low-coordinated CaO surface sites.
summary_en.method: An active-learning-driven DFTB screening stage is coupled with DFT-D3 refinement, periodic slab calculations, and climbing-image NEB barrier estimates.
summary_en.result: Glycerol chemisorbs through bidentate oxygen coordination with spontaneous hydroxyl deprotonation, yielding an adsorption free energy near -32.0 kcal/mol and a low barrier for a second proton transfer.
summary_en.validation: The mechanistic picture is cross-checked against periodic PBE-D3 calculations and ELF/VDD electronic-structure analyses.
